lesson.title: When a Positive Test Doesn't Mean What You Think
lesson.summary: Reversing a conditional probability, going from the chance of evidence given a cause to the chance of the cause given that evidence, can produce a surprisingly different number, especially when the cause is rare.
lesson.body:
P(A given B) and P(B given A) are usually not the same number, and mixing them up is one of the most common reasoning errors in all of probability. The gap between them matters most exactly when one event is rare and the other is common, because a small percentage applied to a huge group can outweigh a large percentage applied to a tiny group. Building intuition for this before you see the formal machinery is the whole point here.

A classic way to build that intuition is to stop thinking in percentages and start thinking in a concrete population of whole people, then count. Imagine, purely as a hypothetical teaching example, a screening test for a rare condition that affects 1 percent of a population. Suppose the test correctly comes back positive for 90 percent of people who truly have the condition, and it also mistakenly comes back positive for 5 percent of people who do not have the condition, a false alarm.

Picture a hypothetical group of 2000 people. Since 1 percent have the condition, that is 20 people with it, and 1980 without it. Among the 20 people with the condition, the test catches 90 percent of them: 20 times 0.90 equals 18 true positives, leaving 2 false negatives. Among the 1980 people without the condition, the test still falsely flags 5 percent of them: 1980 times 0.05 equals 99 false positives, leaving 1881 correct negatives. Every one of these four counts is really the general multiplication rule at work, each is P(a group) times P(positive given that group), just expressed as a headcount instead of a decimal.

Now ask: of everyone who tested positive, what fraction actually has the condition? Total positives are 18 true positives plus 99 false positives, which is 117 people. Only 18 of those 117 actually have the condition, so P(condition given positive) equals 18 divided by 117, which is about 0.154, or roughly 15.4 percent. That is a strange result at first glance. A test that is "90 percent accurate" at catching real cases, and wrong only 5 percent of the time on healthy people, still means a positive result is more likely to be a false alarm than a true finding. The reason is population size: healthy people outnumber sick people by nearly 100 to 1 in this hypothetical, so even a small 5 percent error rate applied to that huge healthy group generates more false alarms, 99 of them, than the 18 true positives coming from the small group who are actually sick.

This is Bayes reasoning in its most intuitive form: you cannot judge P(condition given positive) just by looking at how accurate the test is. You have to weigh that accuracy against how rare the condition was to begin with. The next two sections will show the same reasoning laid out as branches on a tree diagram, which makes the bookkeeping even easier to follow.
